newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian coffee reforms seen delayed until 1998/99.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian coffee reforms seen delayed until 1998/99.

text.p: Ivory Coast will not complete coffee sector reforms until 1998/99 (Oct-Sept) at the earliest but talks with donors on marketing liberalisation have led to some agreement on the way ahead, the World Bank said on Wednesday.
"We are working towards liberalisation of coffee in 1998/99. A lot of interim work needs to be done to prepare the farmers and everyone for it," a World Bank director based in Abidjan told Reuters.
"The government initially thought it wanted to stick to the status quo. But we probably managed to persuade them that that was not particularly positive," he said, referring to private ongoing talks.

The Ivory Coast and donors have met regularly since 1995 to discuss progress with commodity reforms under the terms of a three-tranche $150 million World Bank loan dating back to 1990. The reforms were initially set for the 1997/98 season.
Industry buyers and exporters had also called for renewed liberalisation of coffee marketing, which until the 1995 was controlled by the state Caisse de Stabilisation marketing board.
Since the 1995/96 marketing season the Caistab has set only a guide price for farmers whereas once it dictated prices.
It also phased out upcountry purchasing centres to speed up the flow of produce to Ivory Coast's two main ports, putting in place port-based rather than upcountry quality checks.
The main thrust of liberalisation will depend on which of four proposals put forward by British consultants Landell Mills are finally accepted by donors and the Ivory Coast.

Ivory Coast delayed replying to a preliminary report in January outlining options ranging from maintaining the status quo in different forms to complete liberalisation. A final draft is expected to be ready within weeks.

"The government has replied (until now) that it would prefer option two and I would be surprised if the final version was much different from the preliminary report," said one World Bank official, adding that option two was one form of maintaining the status quo.
World Bank officials have been pushing for acceptance of complete liberalisation of coffee sector marketing and a streamlining of the Caistab to cut administrative costs.
Landell Mills' final report is due to make recommendations on how the Caistab can cut marketing margins through internal competition to below levels in competitor countries.
Advice for further reforms in transportation, quality control and coffee bean hulling is also under review, along with a consideration of forward sales policy.

Local industry buyers and exporters express a clear preference for more liberalisation, saying the Caistab could limit its role to quality assurance and supplying trade information as an industry body.
Exporters and donors are keen to avoid a repeat of plummeting coffee quality seen in other African countries which have accepted donor advice on reducing state board monopolies, analysts said.
Coffee and cocoa quality and price premiums in Cameroon have yet to recover from a boom in the number of buyers and exporters after liberalisation in the early 1990s.
Ivory Coast is set to produce a 1996/97 crop of between 250,000 to 300,000 tonnes, against 180,000 tonnes in 1995/96 and an official 1996/97 forecast of 230,000 tonnes.

Africa's Abidjan-based producers forum, the Interafrican Coffee Organisation (IACO), in a May report put the continent's world market share at 32 percent in 1970-75, with 25 million bags, against 20 percent in 1990-95, with 14.3 million bags.
IACO put the decline down to social and political disruptions, poor incentives and inappropriate macroeconomic frameworks.
Along with donors, the report also cited ageing tree profiles, poor husbandry, and deterioration of research and extension services.
